## Correct, reproducible, and transparent data agents - Sara Altman & Simon Couch

### The core tension: convenience vs. correctness

> In the battle between convenience and correctness, convenience is winning.
>
> — Joe Cheng, Posit CTO

- AI has broadened who can *convincingly* do data analysis, not who can do it *correctly*
- **Opening hypothetical**: a VP asks a coding agent "how is traffic trending?" — the agent picks the wrong table and produces a plausible chart showing a 64% drop, but the real cause was a tracking bug, not an actual decline. A month later nobody can reproduce it (agent history/temp files are gone). Based on a real "vibe analyzing data" pattern Posit has observed.

### Correctness problems predate AI

- https://www.accountingweb.co.uk/business/management-accounting/convivialitys-spreadsheet-hell-sinks-the-business — a spreadsheet error sank a UK beverage wholesaler (Conviviality)
- https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.314.5807.1856 — a sign error in closed-source lab software forced five paper retractions

### Correct *and* convenient — not mutually exclusive

- https://rstudioblog.wordpress.com/2011/02/27/about-the-rstudio-project/ — RStudio's original 2011 mission:

    > Our goal is to develop a powerful tool that supports the practices and techniques required for creating trustworthy, high quality analysis. At the same time, we want RStudio to be as straightforward and intuitive as possible to provide a friendly environment for new and experienced R users alike.
    >
    > — JJ Allaire

- https://posit.co/blog/databot-is-not-a-flotation-device — Databot (Aug 2025, EDA agent in Positron) shipped with an explicit failure-mode warning; Joe Cheng called it his most exciting *and* most dangerous project
- Why keep building despite the risk: curiosity is data science's throughline, and AI tools continue that lineage (like the tidyverse)

### Models are improving, but that alone doesn't fix correctness

- Eval 1: models shown scatterplots with an intentionally reversed relationship — failed as of ~Nov 2025 (described the expected relationship, not the actual one), improved sharply by ~May–Sep 2026
- Eval 2: spotting data-quality issues in a plot (e.g. a suspiciously straight line) — even current top models are still weak here
- Correct analysis also depends on context never in the data itself (dictionaries, tribal knowledge, semantic layers) — has to be curated before a model can use it

### The "slap a human on it" trap

- Human+AI doesn't reliably beat the better of the two alone
- Approval fatigue: people stop reading agent requests and just click approve
- Human trust/judgment shifts with system trust, timing, cognitive load, and social proof — the same expert may decide differently once an agent's involved
- Conclusion: humans should stay in the loop, but the *system* needs to be designed for correctness, not patched with a checkpoint

::: {.callout-important}
## Guiding principle
Help the agent be correct, and make it less bad when it's inevitably sometimes wrong.
:::

### Posit Assistant demo

- Coding agent inside Positron; runs in your actual R/Python session; model/provider-agnostic
- Demo: Houston flight-delay analysis — agent finds the `anyflights` package, reads its docs itself, pulls data
- **Data cleaning mode**: surfaces missing values/outliers as interactive questions (not silent decisions), writes a persistent cleaning script for reproducibility
- Shows plots inline in chat and still flags interpretation limits (checked n=32 before trusting a box plot)
- Can generate a persistent Quarto report via a report-writing skill
- Demo cost $0.05, mostly via GLM 5.3 Flash (~1/30th Opus 5's per-token cost) under the Posit AI Pass — Posit tracks the open-weights cost/capability frontier

### {commons} — new open-source package (launched at this talk)

- https://posit-dev.github.io/commons/
- https://github.com/posit-dev/commons
- https://posit-dev.github.io/commons/r/articles/commons.html
- https://posit-dev.github.io/commons/r/articles/governance.html
- https://opensource.posit.co/blog/2026-09-15_commons-0-1-0/
- Built on Elmer/chatlas/shinychat (R & Python); bring-your-own model
- Core idea: route questions through **trusted code** the team already relies on (packages, Shiny apps, Quarto docs, Databricks/Snowflake semantic views) instead of always generating bespoke code
- Three deterministic response markers: 🟢 trusted calculation, 🔵 cited trusted context, 🟡 freehand code (no trust anchor)
- Deploys as a Shiny app on Connect (normal permissions apply)
- Opt-in OpenTelemetry logging lets the data team spot recurring freehand-fallback questions and promote them into new trusted calculations ("move up the trust ladder")
- Framed beyond VP/business use cases too — biostatisticians/physicians, UX researchers/PMs, policy analysts/program leads
- Thanks: Josh, Talon, Garrick, Aidan/Bowie, Carson Sievert

### Clinical Trials Agent demo

- https://github.com/posit-dev/clinical-trials-agent (simulated data) — trusted code = an internal TLG (tables/listings/graphs) catalog; example query: plot Kaplan-Meier curves

### Closing

- Plausible-looking wrong answers erode trust broadly — AI raises the stakes for correct/transparent/reproducible infrastructure, it doesn't lower the bar
- **Canvas** — teased next-gen agent experience for people who don't want to work in code/an IDE; more from Joe Cheng later that day
- Sara & Simon co-write Posit's biweekly **AI newsletter**

## From chats to workflows to “agents”: Demystifying LLM jargon by example - Timothy Keyes

### Setup

- Speaker: Stanford Healthcare data scientist, also finishing med school
- Colleagues started asking for "agents" for everything instead of "data analysis," making the usual translator role harder — the term had gotten vague/mystical
- Drew from Hadley Wickham's Substack post on agents, the Anthropic Engineering Blog, and OpenAI's Python library

### Live example: patient chart summarizer

- Built live: an LLM system to summarize a (fake, HIPAA-safe) patient's chart before a visit, based on real Stanford Healthcare patterns — test patient has recent lightheadedness
- Compared three systems on the same task:
    - **Simple conversation** (3 lines of code) — fails predictably, no access to the private clinical database
    - **Harness #1 — workflow**: developer-defined steps; map-reduce over notes (map = per-note summary, reduce = meta-summary). Works, but re-reads every note every time (expensive)
    - **Harness #2 — agent**: LLM chooses its own steps via **tools** (list/preview/read notes) in an **agentic loop** — inspects results, decides to call more tools or answer, repeats until done

### Definitions

harness
:   a computer program that coordinates calls to an LLM and other software systems

tool
:   a function the LLM can ask the harness to run on its behalf

agent
:   an LLM within a harness using tools iteratively in a loop until it accomplishes a task

### Evaluation: quality vs. cost

- 10 test queries, scored quality (1–5) vs. cost per query
- Conversation: worst quality (no context). Workflow: good quality, most expensive. Agent: best quality *and* cheapest (only reads relevant notes)
- Caveat: not universal — it's empirical; Stanford Healthcare runs all three patterns in production depending on use case

### Takeaway: three questions before reaching for "agent"

::: {.callout-tip}
1. Do we need an agent, or would a workflow/something simpler work?
2. How should the harness be designed — developer or LLM in control?
3. How will we evaluate whether it works?
:::

- Q&A: stochasticity/variability may belong on your evaluation axis instead of (or with) cost; latency is another common axis

## Yes And...AI in Your IDE - Allissa Dillman & Padmashri Saravanan

- https://github.com/BioDataSage/yesand

### Core question: does agreement mean correctness?

- Opening bit: an LLM "yes, and"s every bad decision about how to give a conference talk
- When an LLM agrees with you, is it because your reasoning is sound, or because it's picked up patterns of confidence/tone/deference from training data?
- Cited research: politely-phrased questions scored 80.8% accuracy vs. 84.8% for rudely-phrased ones — a supposedly-irrelevant factor shifted performance
- Code review isn't enough: most LLM coding failures are bad planning/reasoning, not syntax — "plausible code for the wrong analysis." Need to vet the question and framing, not just the code
- IDE-based assistants have more context and proactively suggest next steps — so the model shapes the next question too, not just answers the current one

### Persona study (NYC Squirrel Count dataset)

- Gave Posit Assistant the same vague prompt ("I am a [persona], clean this data for me") across three personas on a fixed dataset/task
- Dataset: 2020 NYC Squirrel Count (72 volunteers, 433 sightings, 24 parks) — messy, mixed structured/unstructured
- Categorized every change the AI made: preserved / transformed / interpreted / discarded
    - Data manager → preserved most, fewest destructive changes
    - Data science student → more transformations, optimizing for a faster path to analysis
    - Environmental researcher → dropped the most data, made the most assumptions

::: {.callout-warning}
## Irreversible by default
Some of these choices are irreversible — a silent NA conversion or a discarded detail — even though the code still runs fine and looks correct.
:::

### Fix: skills that surface decisions earlier

- Example 4-skill pipeline: analytics metrics → planning a data vis → accessible visualization → Quarto report
- Problem with review-only feedback: by the time you see a draft, the analytical direction is locked in — feedback becomes revision, not decision-making

::: {.callout-tip}
## "Pause, ask, follow directions" skill design rules
1. Only pause on decisions that change the question/method/story/interpretation
2. Give just enough context to decide
3. Never editorialize ("great choice," "are you sure?") — present the options and follow the user's direction
:::

- Demo: asking about report focus/audience/metric/chart specifics up front produced specific, meaningful output (e.g. density rankings, a borough with disproportionately more cinnamon squirrels) instead of a generic default chart

### Limitations

- A visible decision isn't automatically an informed one — domain expertise still matters
- Too many pauses create fatigue; the model still controls which options are surfaced and how
- Technical experience alone doesn't guarantee people can evaluate AI outputs well
- Closing: treat model agreement as a prompt to interrogate assumptions/context/defaults, not the end of reasoning

## Hello, robot: Introducing humans to LLM’s - Kristin Bott

- https://github.com/posit-dev/ai-intro

### Case study: Brittany

- Accounts payable specialist (non-engineer) on Posit's finance team; built Claude skills over 6 months to draft finance entries and parse bills — saves 5–10 hrs/week, no sensitive data sent to Anthropic
- Central question: how do you teach non-engineers to work effectively with AI?
- Origin: 2025 Posit engineering LLM hackathons excited engineers but left the rest of the org unaddressed

### "Intro to AI at Posit" course

- Built with colleague Garrick, aimed at non-engineers
- Goals: accurate mental models of how LLMs work, a sense of where they succeed/fail, conversational fluency, more effective use
- Format: 5 hrs total over one week, groups of 10–14 from across the org, no homework, voluntary
- Approach: strip away tooling/conveniences so learners see raw mechanics first — "words in, words out" before formal definitions
- Garrick built custom apps so learners could *experience* concepts directly (stochasticity via regenerating a prompt, tokens via color-coded output) before naming them

### Key exercises & demos

- Failure modes covered: hallucinated-but-plausible library functions, and LLMs not correcting a false premise

::: {.callout-note}
## Model knowledge vs. tool capability
A raw model can't answer "who's keynoting posit::conf," but Claude Desktop can — not because the model knows, but because its web-search tool found it. Separate what the model knows from what the harness/tooling can do (echoes Timothy Keyes's harness talk).
:::

- Exercise: predicted LLM success vs. task difficulty, then tested by counting "n"s in "unconventional" — asking directly vs. asking for code that counts. Code won clearly (tokens ≠ letters)

### Outcomes

> This class gave me a conceptual foundation that removed my fear. It gave me permission to try. And then I realized building tools was something I could actually do.
>
> — Brittany

- 120+ Posit employees have taken the course; curriculum posted publicly
- Closing pitch: small-group, safe-environment training focused on experience/curiosity is worth it
- Q&A (James Wade): best practices go stale fast — durable foundational mental models transfer even as specific tips/tools change

## From Tribal Knowledge to Trusted AI in Pharma - Tanya Cashorali

### Setup

- Speaker runs TCB Analytics (founded 2015), ~20 years using R
- Opening bit: "is a hot dog a sandwich?" — running metaphor for definitional disagreement, revisited at the close
- Client: a pharma company (rare disease/cancer therapies) wanted an agent to help sales reps answer data questions faster in the field
- Core lesson: the hard part wasn't the technical build — it was figuring out what people meant and encoding scattered tribal knowledge (heads, Shiny apps, spreadsheets) into the model

> If you don't talk to humans first, AI is a great way to automate misunderstandings.

### Discovery: talking to the sales reps first

- Had reps log real day-to-day questions in a spreadsheet rather than guessing what to build
- Existing workflow: several siloed Shiny apps (some separated for compliance), manual filter/export cycle taking ~30 min per answer
- Interviews surfaced hidden complexity:
    - "Called on" meant *any* interaction (call, email, Zoom, in-office), not just phone calls
    - "Active patient" needed an explicit definition (shipment received, not discontinued, within a time window)
    - Reps disagreed on scope (one wanted specialty-distributor patients — a source not even in Snowflake yet) and on time windows ("recently" = 30 vs. 60 days)

### Building trusted data products

- Recurring question patterns became reusable Snowflake tables for the agent to query — compared directly to the "trusted queries" idea from the morning keynote ({commons})
- Business logic encoded as explicit flags (e.g. `is_active`, `called_last_30_days`) to reduce SQL errors and give safe, flexible building blocks
- More tribal knowledge pulled in: a manually-updated spreadsheet owned by one person (monthly sales-lead consensus), and logic already embedded in Shiny apps (manual doctor exclusions, "center of excellence" flags)
- Pipeline: client script converts spreadsheets/manual adjustments to Parquet/CSV → scheduled R script on Posit Connect loads it into Snowflake, with failure-email alerts

### Semantic layer

- A Snowflake YAML config taught the AI to "speak the business's language": definitions (patient, quarter-to-date incl. a non-standard fiscal calendar), rules, synonyms/abbreviations (e.g. "PTS" = patients, drug slang), and entity relationships/joins across a billion-row dataset

### Feedback loop & trust

- Released as a chatbot; thumbs up/down plus a reason fed straight into fixes (sometimes shipped the next day)
- Success example: an open-ended trip-planning question ("how should I plan my trip to San Antonio?") combined multiple business rules into a genuinely useful answer
- Issues fixed via feedback: domain jargon (e.g. "BID dosing" = twice daily), a wrong call count traced to "seen"/"contacted"/"live" ambiguity, missing "center of excellence" data
- Trust emerged because: fast visible feedback loop, the system spoke their language, and it ran on data/logic they already trusted (years of manual Shiny-app exclusions)

### Closing

- Returns to the hot dog question: the better question isn't the classification, it's "why do we need to classify it, and what decision are we making with the answer?" A question that can't drive a decision is just "making pretty pictures for fun." The AI doesn't get to decide definitions — the organization does

::: {.callout-important}
## Closing message
Talk to humans first, agree on what words mean, then make sure it's a question worth answering — in that order.
:::

## What Context Do Your AI Agents Actually Need - Sharon Wang

### Reframing the question

- The durable question isn't "what context do agents need" but "what context do *you* need" — that holds even as models/harnesses/best practices keep changing
- 92 frontier LLMs released in 2025, ~127 projected for 2026; release rate up 4x+ since 2023 — even Positron's own context-management best practices from a year ago have had to be abandoned
- You can't write down for an agent what you don't understand yourself — domain expertise is what makes AI-assisted analysis correct, not just plausible-looking

### Building your own understanding

- Inventory what you already know: what question you're answering, where the data came from, what a row represents, who else knows about this, constraints/deadlines, and any trusted code to reference (ties to the {commons} keynote)
- Write down goals and ideal outcomes for *yourself* before starting, not for the agent — prevents scope creep and endless goalpost-moving during review

### Managing context day to day

- Context sources: what you paste in chat, what the harness auto-grabs (system prompt, IDE state, console, schema), files you write in advance (AGENTS.md, skills, memory), and on-demand context (file search, MCP)
- Write understanding into project context files/AGENTS.md instead of re-explaining every session; use a Save Memory skill for learnings, a Create Skill skill for recurring workflows
- Reference file paths instead of pasting full file contents — lets the agent search only what it needs, cuts token usage
- Prefer text/file references over images/screenshots — models spend more tokens reconstructing pixels than reading text directly
- For live data in an app, connect via MCP rather than pasting exports (points ahead to Neal Richardson's talk)

::: {.callout-tip}
## When to start a new chat
A new task, a side quest, or catching yourself re-explaining in circles are all signs to start fresh rather than push through a degraded context window.
:::

### Building collaboratively

- Build a shared team "understanding inventory," then translate it into shared context files — make space (team meetings, pairing, 1:1s) to discuss what is/isn't working with AI tooling
- Revisit team workflows and habits regularly: some pre-agent habits no longer fit, others got dropped and should come back
- Q&A: stale AGENTS.md/memory files are best caught by noticing recurring frustration/repetition as a team — this can also be encoded into a skill that keeps them updated

## AI Agents Deserve R - James Wade

### Framing: a coherent ecosystem, not the largest one

- Recurring worry: "am I sacrificing capability by staying in R instead of Python/Claude Code?" — reframed to only switch language when there's a compelling reason, not by default
- Agents don't need the largest ecosystem, they need a coherent one — that requirement falls on the developer (to hold a deep mental model of what they're building), since models already understand Python/JS well from training data

### Demo: "real", a personal RSS reader

- Built to fix generic AI daily-briefing tools: an LLM-driven "orientation" step ranks/filters articles and explains its reasoning, plus lightweight feedback (dismiss/engage) and a chat interface over individual articles or the full corpus
- Built almost entirely from a small set of R packages, each contributing one distinct piece

### Ecosystem tour

- **Shiny Chat** (R & Python): conversation history (resume/search/rename/fork), exposed thinking traces with an interrupt button, dynamic tool-call display, slash commands reusable for in-app navigation — "a few lines of code" to add to any Shiny app
- **Elmer**: LLM interfacing; new tool annotations let you flag a tool as read-only vs. world-affecting for downstream safety
- **Deputy** (new, built on Elmer): adds permissions and usage limits on top of Elmer's tool-calling classes — enterprise-style safety controls
- **DSPR**: an R port of Python's DSPy ("programming, not prompting") — define modules/signatures for inputs/outputs, then apply optimization algorithms against a scoring metric to auto-update prompts as models change, instead of manually rewriting them each release

### Closing

- Staying in R does mean missing out on some things — but the gaps are small enough to see and to build/contribute to yourself, since agents make porting a Python capability into an R package cheap
- Encouraged the audience to build and contribute to the R agent ecosystem

## MCP, or not MCP - Neal Richardson

- https://enpiar.com/mcp-posit-conf-2026/#/section

### The problem: Zendesk tickets Claude couldn't read

- Posit's enterprise products run on customer infrastructure — support tickets (Zendesk) are the engineering team's only window into a customer issue, and reconstructing context from a ticket was manual and slow
- Wanted to hand Claude Code a ticket URL directly, but hit two walls: no safe way to give it Zendesk credentials, and Zendesk's REST API isn't shaped for efficient/secure agent use

### What MCP actually is

- Fundamentally simple: a standard for hosting tools (functions + descriptions) for LLMs to call, and for clients to query them — "just another API standard," tailored to AI applications
- Local MCP servers run on your machine; remote ones are shared via a URL — talk focuses on writing your own remote server

### MCP vs. CLI vs. skills

- Skills = plain instructions/context; enough on their own if the agent's existing tools (shell, web requests) can already do the job
- A CLI beats MCP when the CLI already exists, is widely used, and is in the model's training data (e.g. `gh`) — no context spent teaching the model how to use it
- A custom MCP server beats a new/custom CLI: a new CLI isn't in training data (costs the same context to teach it) and has its own distribution problem (everyone must install it)
- Using an existing personal-auth CLI (e.g. `gh`) means the agent can do anything you personally can on that service — harder to scope down than a purpose-built MCP tool

::: {.callout-warning}
## The lethal trifecta (Simon Willison)
An agent combining (1) access to private data, (2) exposure to untrusted content, and (3) the ability to communicate out can be tricked into exfiltrating private data via prompt injection — surprisingly easy to satisfy, e.g. reading a public GitHub issue (untrusted content) with an agent that also has private repo access and web-request ability.
:::

### Best practices for writing your own MCP server

1. Only define the tools you need — less context, less chance the agent picks the wrong tool, and fewer dangerous tools to misuse (be especially careful with write/delete tools)
2. Keep responses concise — strip anything from an upstream API response that isn't needed for the task, since everything returned goes into context
3. Practice data hygiene — strip or redact PII/unneeded fields from API responses to reduce exposure

### Demo: Zendesk MCP server on Posit Connect

- Built with the `fastmcp` Python library, deployed to Connect like any other app
- Connect handles Zendesk auth via a built-in integration (negotiates credentials on demand, no long-lived API key stored anywhere) and exposes an OAuth flow to Claude Code
- Connect's MCP view lists available servers/tools with runnable descriptions, plus usage monitoring (who's using what, when)

::: {.callout-important}
## Guiding principle
Remote MCP servers are cheap to write today — write narrow ones for exactly what you need, since narrow tools "leave prompt injection with empty hands," and let Connect handle auth, governance, and monitoring.
:::

## Why Is AI Costing Me So Much Money? - Winston Chang

### LLM cost mechanics

- LLMs are stateless — each request resends the *entire* prior conversation; there's no persistent "mind" holding context between turns
- Context length (tokens per request) grows roughly linearly over a conversation, but total cost is the cumulative sum of every request — so total spend grows quadratically (like a parabola) with conversation length
- Output tokens typically cost ~5x input tokens

::: {.callout-tip}
## Caching is the biggest lever
If a request's input tokens repeat an earlier request's input tokens in the same order, the repeated portion is served from cache at roughly 1/10th the normal input-token cost.
:::

### Why coding agents specifically got expensive

- A single user request can fan out into many agentic-loop round trips (tool call → result → tool call → ...), each resending the growing conversation — this, more than raw model pricing, is what drove costs up over the last year

### Cost controls

- Subscription plans (Claude Pro/Max, OpenAI Plus/Pro) can be worth up to 10x the token allowance vs. pay-as-you-go retail pricing — great for individuals, but usually unusable for enterprises needing data-privacy guarantees (subscription usage can be logged/trained on)
- Posit AI Pass offers zero-data-retention (ZDR) agreements across its models, trading away the deep subscription discounts for that guarantee
- Make cost visible: Positron Assistant shows running conversation cost plus a detailed breakdown; Wes McKinney's **Agents View** tool (local, self-hosted) tracks and lets you search cost across conversations
- Start a new conversation once you pivot to an unrelated task, instead of paying to resend the unrelated earlier context every turn (Positron Assistant's token counter turns red on long conversations as a nudge)
- Pick a cheaper model when the task allows it — e.g. Haiku (half of Sonnet), GPT-5.6 Luna (~1/10th of Sonnet, "more capable than Haiku 4.5"), GLM 5.3 Flash (~1/20th of Sonnet) — good for interactive/non-agentic coding, not full agentic loops
- Write plans/reports/handoff docs to markdown instead of extending one long conversation; a **handoff document** (explicit continuation notes plus a ready-to-paste next prompt) gives more control than `/compact`'s automatic summary
- Thinking/reasoning tokens count as output tokens; continuing a thinking trace in a later turn requires resending its identifier, which then counts as full input tokens again

### Closing

- Q&A: caching support depends on the serving software, not just the model — e.g. not consistently present when running open-weights models locally via Ollama/LM Studio
